fetched_contents.text: Associations Between Socioeconomic Factors and Alcohol Outcomes Abstract Socioeconomic status (SES) is one of the many factors influencing a person’s alcohol use and related outcomes. Findings have indicated that people with higher SES may consume similar or greater amounts of alcohol compared with people with lower SES, although the latter group seems to bear a disproportionate burden of negative alcohol-related consequences. These associations are further complicated by a variety of moderating factors, such as race, ethnicity, and gender. Thus, among individuals with lower SES, members of further marginalized communities, such as racial and ethnic minorities and homeless individuals, experience greater alcohol-related consequences. Future studies are needed to more fully explore the underlying mechanisms of the relationship between SES and alcohol outcomes. This knowledge should be applied toward the development of multilevel interventions that address not only individual-level risks but also economic disparities that have precipitated and maintained a disproportionate level of alcohol-related consequences among more marginalized and vulnerable populations. Keywords: Alcohol consumption, alcohol-related problems, alcohol-related consequences, special populations, socioeconomic status, socioeconomic factors, economic disparities, racial minority, ethnic minority, homeless ---------------------------------------- According to the World Health Organization (2014), alcohol consumption is responsible for approximately 5.9 percent of deaths worldwide and a global loss of 139 million disability-adjusted life-years. The alcohol-related disease burden is precipitated in part by acute intoxication, which decreases reaction time, perception and motor skills, and inhibitions and is thereby associated with an increased risk for traffic accidents, self-inflicted injuries, suicide, falls, drownings, alcohol poisoning, and interpersonal violence. Longer-term effects of alcohol consumption also contribute to the disease burden by way of various medical conditions (e.g., cancer, cardiovascular disease, and liver cirrhosis) and psychiatric disorders (e.g., depression and alcohol use disorder [AUD]). Given the strong positive association between alcohol use and negative alcohol-related consequences, it is important to understand social determinants of these alcohol outcomes. The quantity and frequency of a person’s alcohol use, the resulting negative alcohol-related consequences (also known as alcohol-related problems), and his or her risk of AUD are determined by a variety of influences. These include higher-level chrono- and macrolevel factors, such as historical time and geopolitical context, as well as meso-, micro-, and individual-level factors, such as community context, family/peer influences, biological predisposition, effects of prenatal alcohol exposure, psychological factors, and sociodemographic features (e.g., gender, age, race, ethnicity, culture, religious affiliation, and socioeconomic status [SES]) (Edwards 2000; Gately 2008). These factors, which operate within various systems and levels, interact and transact over time to determine alcohol-related outcomes, such as drinking patterns and negative alcohol-related consequences (Gruenewald et al. 2014; Holder 1998). This article focuses on one particular aspect of this complex set of systems, namely the relationship between SES—including income/economic factors, educational level, employment status, and housing status—and alcohol-related outcomes. It synthesizes data primarily obtained from English-language systematic reviews and meta-analyses that were based on studies conducted in the past decade involving adult populations (for a summary of these reviews and meta-analyses, see table 1). In some cases, these analyses were limited to studies from only one country, whereas other analyses were cross-national. In any case, caution must be used when interpreting these findings, because the cultural and political contexts in which these phenomena occur can differ widely. In addition, this article reviews some larger, population-based studies (see table 2), particularly those that were not addressed within the included reviews and which directly assess the association between SES and alcohol consumption and related outcomes. Although most of the studies only included adults, a few also involved adolescents when meta-analyses and reviews did not exclude such studies. Table 1. fetched_contents.text: Systemic inequities in alcohol licensing: Case studies in eight Aotearoa New Zealand communities Abstract Introduction Many countries, including Aotearoa New Zealand, have socioeconomic and ethnic inequities in alcohol outlet density, yet the potential contribution of alcohol licensing systems is almost unexplored. After licensing reforms in Aotearoa in 2012, community groups and Māori (the Indigenous people) continued to struggle to influence decisions, prompting calls for reform and authority for Māori reflecting Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations. This study explored factors in the failure of public objections in under‐resourced neighbourhoods. Methods In a descriptive, multimethod qualitative study, we analysed eight decisions to grant off‐licence approvals in socioeconomically deprived areas. Each licence was opposed. Hearing participants and local residents were interviewed. Data were thematically analysed to identify factors affecting objector influence, alignment with Indigenous rights and residents' awareness of alcohol issues and licensing processes. Results Residents identified relevant local harms but were largely unaware of opportunities to object. Objectors faced structural barriers to accessing and influencing hearings that were exacerbated by resource challenges, including travel costs, lost income, competing social issues and limited legal representation. Evidence of area deprivation supported objectors' arguments regarding risk, but a lack of official data on harms undermined them. Māori input was excluded by legal barriers and failures to recognise relevant rights and elements of culture. Discussion and Conclusions Structural barriers, including racism, restricted the influence of under‐resourced communities and Māori in licensing decisions and weakened risk assessment, which may hinder community efforts to reduce their disproportionate exposure to alcohol outlets. Licensing systems should be reviewed from equity and Indigenous perspectives. Keywords: alcohol licensing, alcohol outlet density, Indigenous rights, inequity, structural racism 1. INTRODUCTION The disproportionately high concentration of off‐licence alcohol retail outlets in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas is a longstanding social injustice in several high‐income countries, including Aotearoa New Zealand [1, 2, 3, 4]. Ethnic inequities are also apparent here; neighbourhoods with a higher‐than‐average proportion of Māori (the Indigenous people) residents have 32% more alcohol outlets than those with a lower proportion [5]. Relationships between alcohol outlet density and violent offences are well established [6], and a growing body of studies show that off‐licence outlet density is positively associated with violence, crime, public disorder, property damage and reduced amenity [7]. Surveys of harm caused by others' drinking from several countries suggest this alcohol‐related disorder disproportionately affects how safe women and younger people feel in public spaces [8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. Off‐licence density is also linked to increased consumption and higher‐risk drinking patterns [13]; for instance, greater off‐licence density has been associated with increased risky and heavy‐episodic drinking among lower‐income groups but not high‐income groups in Scotland, possibly because people with less income spend more time in their neighbourhood [14]. Variations in alcohol outlet distribution may therefore contribute to the socioeconomic inequities found in alcohol attributable mortality [15]. As alcohol licensing systems impact availability, it is relevant to assess their role in the inequitable distribution of retail outlets. Some studies indicate lower rents may attract alcohol retailers to lower‐income areas, particularly if near wealthier areas with higher demand for alcohol [16, 17]. Others have suggested residents with less income have less capacity to prevent new outlets opening due to having lower residential stability, financial resources and social capital to draw on in engaging in planning and licensing processes [18]; however, inequities within such processes have seldom been studied. In Aotearoa New Zealand, concern over the proliferation of off‐licence outlets in socioeconomically deprived areas was recognised in the development of the Sale and Supply of Alcohol Act 2012 (‘the Act’), which was intended to give communities more say over where alcohol is sold [19]. The Act enabled licence objections based on alcohol's impact on amenity and disorder and introduced a new harm minimisation objective. However, public objections remained largely unsuccessful [20], and many local governments struggled to use new powers to restrict new licences in specific areas through Local Alcohol Policies, which may limit outlet density and proximity to sensitive sites [21]. In addition, the Government has been challenged for failing to support Māori authority in decisions about alcohol, contrary to Government commitments to uphold Māori self‐determination set out in Te Tiriti o Waitangi (‘Te Tiriti’ – the Māori language version of the treaty between Māori and the British Crown that is the founding document of New Zealand) and despite alcohol harm being disproportionately high among Māori in the colonial context [22, 23]. This study examined the factors influencing the outcome of community objections to off‐licence applications for alcohol‐specific retail outlets (i.e. liquor stores) in socioeconomically deprived communities. These are often small‐scale stores, which typically serve local residents and sell all types of alcohol products (grocery or supermarkets in Aotearoa New Zealand only sell beer and wine). The study builds on a prior legal analysis by LG, which identified four areas of legal argument in off‐licence hearings that affect the outcome of public objections [24]. 2. Several neighborhood contextual factors may be important aspects of this “alcohol environment.” Methods Participants were 15,197 young adults (age 18–26) from Wave III of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health, a nationally-representative United States survey. Measures of past-year alcohol use and problems were obtained via structured in-home interviews. Tract-level neighborhood contextual factors (density of on- and off-premises alcohol outlets, neighborhood disadvantage, rural versus urban residence) were derived from census indicators and geocoded state-level alcohol outlet licenses. Multivariate logistic regression, ordered logistic regression, or negative binomial regression models, including age, sex, race, and household income as covariates, were fit to examine the relation of the neighborhood contextual factors with alcohol use and problems. Results The most consistent finding across four of the five measures of alcohol involvement was their association with neighborhood advantage; the active ingredient underlying this effect was primarily the proportion of educated residents in the neighborhood. The densities of alcohol outlets were associated with any alcohol use – they were not associated with binge drinking or alcohol problems, nor could they explain any of the neighborhood advantage effects. The influence of alcohol outlet densities on alcohol involvement did not differ for those above or below the legal age to purchase alcohol. Living in a rural versus an urban neighborhood was associated with a different alcohol use pattern characterized by a lower likelihood of any drinking, but among those who drank, consuming more alcohol per occasion. Conclusions Living in a more advantaged and educated urban neighborhood with greater densities of bars and restaurants is associated with greater alcohol involvement among 18–26-year-olds in the United States. This geographic variation is a clue that there may be important environmental factors contributing to alcohol involvement. Several neighborhood contextual factors, such as alcohol outlet density, neighborhood disadvantage, and rural versus urban residence may be important aspects of this “alcohol environment.” Neighborhood alcohol outlet density The most widely-discussed contributor to the “alcohol environment” is availability (Gruenewald et al., 2002; Gruenewald, 2011; Popova et al., 2009), in particular, the regional density of alcohol outlets (Campbell et al., 2009; Gruenewald, 2007). Alcohol availability theory posits that greater outlet density increases alcohol consumption by reducing the effective price of alcohol, that is, by decreasing the time and effort (“convenience costs”) of obtaining alcohol (Stockwell & Gruenewald, 2004). One of the ways in which geographic variation in alcohol involvement can arise is because alcohol outlet density is regulated at the state, and sometimes, at the local level (Treno et al., 2014). There remain major gaps in the evidence base on the association between neighborhood alcohol outlet density and alcohol use and problems. In the United States, other than two studies across college campuses (Weitzman et al., 2003; Scribner et al., 2008), the studies have been regional. The alcohol outcomes are often limited to assessments of alcohol use rather than problems and focus almost exclusively on urban neighborhoods. Most studies conducted in the United States have yielded positive associations (Brenner et al., 2015; Gruenewald et al., 2002; Gruenewald et al., 2014; Schonlau et al., 2008; Scribner et al., 2000; Truong & Sturm, 2007), but studies have also yielded negative (Gruenewald et al., 2002), and no association (Pollack et al., 2005; Schonlau et al., 2008; Truong & Sturm, 2007) between outlet density and alcohol consumption. This suggests that alcohol use and problems may be greater in disadvantaged than in advantaged neighborhoods because of easier access to alcohol. fetched_contents.text: Older Māori understandings of alcohol use in Aotearoa/New Zealand Introduction Indigenous people’s alcohol use is often understood in relation to the dominant public health understanding of ‘problem alcohol use’. This master narrative is routinely drawn on to explain the negative impacts of alcohol on indigenous people’s health (Bjerregaard, Young, Dewailly, & Ebbesson, 2004; Durie, 2004; Hudson, 2011; Saggers & Gray, 1998; Seale, Shellenberger, Rodriguez, Seale, & Alvarado, 2002). Similarly, in Aotearoa (New Zealand), it is widely acknowledged that alcohol use has had deleterious effects on the health and wellbeing of Māori (indigenous people of Aotearoa) (Durie, 2004; Dyall et al., 2014; Ministry of Health, 2013, Ministry of Health, 2016). For example, epidemiological research suggests Māori are more likely to engage in hazardous and/or binge drinking alcohol use (Bramley et al., 2003; Connor, Kydd, Shield, & Rehm, 2015); that a high number of older Māori engage in hazardous alcohol use (Herbert & Stephens, 2015); and, that Māori suffer more harm in comparison to non-Māori (Connor et al., 2015; Moewaka Barnes, McPherson, & Bhatta, 2003). Accordingly, alcohol policy and interventions have regularly sought to reduce problematic alcohol use among Māori (Durie, 2004; Gray, Pulver, Saggers & Waldon, 2006; Inter-Agency Committee on Drugs, 2015; Huriwai, 2002; Saggers & Gray, 1998), by drawing on causal theories of alcohol misuse (Durie, 2004; Durie & Soutar, 2001; Marie, Fergusson, & Boden, 2012 Saggers & Gray, 1998). In contrast, there has been little exploration of how Māori contextualise and understand their alcohol use. Globally, socially acceptable alcohol norms and behaviors are largely determined by dominant western cultures, and applied to explanations of indigenous alcohol use (Sargent, 1983; Spicer, Novins, Mitchell, & Beals, 2003), resulting in divergent ideas between indigenous and Western cultures around what constitutes acceptable or problematic, alcohol use. This may contribute to the development and maintenance of negative stereotypes and misconceptions (Byron, 1996; Hall & Hunter, 1995; Hudson, 2011; Hunter, 1993; May, 1996; Spicer et al., 2003; Westermeyer, 1979; Whitbeck Chen, Hoyt, & Adams, 2004). Despite a lack of empirical data to support such stereotypes (e.g. May, 1996; Spicer et al., 2003), and the acknowledged diversity of alcohol use among indigenous populations (e.g. Byron 1996; Hanson, 1995; Hunter, 1993; Westermeyer, 1979), these stereotypes persist. They contribute to dominant ideas that any alcohol use among indigenous people must be hazardous and, have detrimental social and health effects (Byron, 1996; Hunter, 1993; Lurie, 1979; Saggers & Gray, 1998). The reliance on the ‘problem alcohol use’ narrative results in disparate ideas between indigenous and western cultures about what constitutes ‘problematic’ alcohol use. For example, in Tahiti, French authorities raised concerns about indigenous Tahitian people’s alcohol use, in particular, their spending the majority of their income on alcohol rather than on housing and material self-improvement, which were deemed more important by the French. However, indigenous Tahitian people did not value material possessions in the same way as the French. Rather, many viewed alcohol as an indulgent pleasure and a reward for working (Lemert, 1979). Lemert thus challenged the French views of this as problematic alcohol use, questioning, “Whose hierarchies are being invoked when the costs of drinking are assessed?” (p. 199). In recognition of the value that an indigenous perspective would provide, Brough, Bond and Hunt (2004) argue for the need to develop “resources and strategies which connect appropriately to the social and cultural spaces occupied by Indigenous people” (p. 216). In Aotearoa, Durie (1998) has identified the need for a bottom up approach whereby involvement in Māori communities operates from a Māori philosophical base in order to achieve successful health promotion outcomes. Such approaches rely on culturally responsive and appropriate alcohol policy to support them. It has been argued that ideas about health are often founded upon Western notions of health and wellbeing, which in turn, inform health policy and promotion initiatives (King, Smith & Gracey, 2009; Ratima, 2001), and this may limit their effectiveness among Māori (Brady, 2000; Gray & Saggers, 2005; Ratima, 2001; Wood, France, Hunt, Eades, & Slack-Smith, 2008). This recognition is supported by the continued disparities observed in Māori health and wellbeing outcomes when compared to non-Māori (Ratima, 2001, p. 110). Alcohol policy and interventions among Māori are apparently failing, with minimal change in harmful alcohol use observed over the last 20 years (Alcohol Advisory Council of New Zealand & MOH, 2001; Ministry of Health, 2009, Ministry of Health, 2016). Alcohol policy and health promotion practice must adapt to the cultural preferences and social realities of Māori while also supporting secure identities (and other Māori identified goals) to improve overall lifestyles among Māori (Ratima, 2001; Ropiha, 1994; Walton, Tu’Itahi, Stairmand, & Neely, 2015). Moreover, health professionals must attend to and foreground indigenous counter narratives to dominant ‘western’ narratives, which often proceed from a position of cultural superiority or ethnocentrism. To this end, research regarding Māori conceptualisations of alcohol use can strengthen alcohol policy and health promotion efforts aimed at addressing issues associated with alcohol use among Māori. Our study aimed to explore older Māori perspectives on alcohol use, to broaden current understandings. In acknowledgment of the collective wisdom of Māori elders (Durie, 1999; Kukutai, 2006; Maaka, 1993), we specifically sought the combined knowledge of groups of older Māori to provide a greater depth of understanding of alcohol use. Main socio-economic drivers of hazardous drinking among Māori

The evidence points to a pattern in which socioeconomic status (SES), particularly through income, education, and neighborhood disadvantage, is consistently associated with drinking risk, though the direction of association can vary by population and measure. The most consistent findings across the search material are that people with lower SES may bear a disproportionate burden of negative alcohol-related consequences, while people with higher SES may consume similar or greater amounts of alcohol compared with lower SES groups [N1-F1]. A review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses also states that socioeconomic factors—including income, education, employment status, and housing status—are among the many influences on alcohol use and related outcomes [N1-F1].

For income, the evidence is broad and mixed in the general population, but the dominant theme is that lower income is often linked to greater alcohol-related harm rather than necessarily greater consumption. The review explicitly notes that lower gross national income was associated with more alcohol-related consequences in men in a cross-national study, and that lower educational attainment was associated with more reported alcohol-related consequences [N1-F1]. A related source states that people with lower socioeconomic status are disproportionately affected by alcohol-related harms [N4-R3]. This suggests income is a strong explanatory variable for hazardous drinking and related harms, but not necessarily for consumption alone.

Education also appears to matter. The same cross-national study linked lower educational attainment to more alcohol-related consequences [N1-F1]. A separate source on neighborhood context found that living in a more advantaged and educated urban neighborhood was associated with greater alcohol involvement among young adults, though outlet density was not consistently linked to binge drinking or alcohol problems [N4-F3]. This indicates education and neighborhood advantage are important contextual factors, but the evidence is more consistent for harm and involvement than for simple drinking quantity.

Employment status is present in the SES literature but not as directly emphasized in the provided evidence. The SES review explicitly includes employment status as part of SES, but the evidence excerpt does not provide a direct Māori-specific finding on employment alone [N1-F1]. A neighborhood study did find that rural versus urban residence shaped alcohol use patterns, with rural residents less likely to drink but more likely to drink heavily when they did [N4-F3]. This suggests employment-related mobility or stability may influence drinking risk through neighborhood structure and rural/urban contexts, but the evidence is indirect.

When it comes to deprivation versus relative disadvantage, the evidence supports the latter as a better explanatory frame. The neighborhood study found that the most consistent association was with neighborhood advantage, with the active ingredient being the proportion of educated residents in the neighborhood [N4-F3]. Another source notes that area-level socioeconomic status and alcohol involvement studies produced mixed findings, with neighborhood advantage and disadvantage each appearing in roughly similar proportions of studies [N4-F3]. This implies that relative disadvantage or contextual disadvantage should be treated as a stronger explanatory frame than absolute deprivation, because neighborhood advantage and disadvantage can produce opposite or mixed effects depending on local conditions.

Overall, the socio-economic variables most consistently associated with hazardous drinking are income, education, and neighborhood disadvantage/advantage [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Income and education are important because they are linked to greater alcohol-related harm and to contextual drinking involvement [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Deprivation or relative disadvantage is the better explanatory frame because neighborhood advantage and disadvantage both appear as significant contextual factors and the evidence suggests neighborhood advantage can drive greater alcohol involvement, while disadvantage is often associated with greater outlet density and risk [N4-F3][N4-R2]. The evidence is strongest for harm and involvement rather than consumption alone, and for neighborhood and contextual SES rather than individual SES alone [N1-F1][N4-F3].

Historical, structural, and cultural context shaping Māori drinking patterns

The evidence strongly points to colonization, historical disadvantage, and structural inequities as foundational drivers of current Māori drinking patterns. A case study on alcohol licensing in eight Aotearoa New Zealand communities notes that the disproportionately high concentration of off-licence alcohol retail outlets in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas is a longstanding social injustice, and that Māori communities and under-resourced communities continue to struggle to influence licensing decisions [N2-F2]. It also states that the proliferation of alcohol outlets in deprived areas is linked to increased consumption and higher-risk drinking patterns, and that structural barriers, including racism, restricted the influence of Māori in licensing decisions [N2-F2]. These findings indicate that historical disadvantage is not a relic of the past but an ongoing structural condition that shapes current alcohol availability and harm.

Colonization is explicitly tied to Māori drinking patterns in the evidence. The same licensing study says that alcohol harm is disproportionately high among Māori in the colonial context and that Māori input was excluded by legal barriers and failures to recognize relevant rights and culture [N2-F2]. Another source states that longstanding issues over heavy consumption, alcohol addiction, alcohol dependence, and alcohol-related harm can reasonably be linked back to the colonising context [N2-R5]. This historical framing suggests that colonial dispossession, disrupted social structures, and ongoing inequities have created conditions in which alcohol-related harm is concentrated among Māori.

Whānau, tikanga, and cultural identity are also central to understanding Māori drinking behavior. The evidence on older Māori understandings of alcohol use emphasizes that indigenous people’s alcohol use is often understood through dominant public health narratives of “problem alcohol use,” but that this narrative often ignores how Māori themselves contextualize and understand alcohol use [N5-F4]. The study stresses that socially acceptable alcohol norms are largely determined by dominant western cultures, and that this creates divergent ideas between indigenous and Western cultures around what constitutes acceptable or problematic alcohol use [N5-F4]. It also argues that health policy and interventions must adapt to Māori cultural preferences and social realities while supporting secure identities [N5-F4]. This indicates that whānau and tikanga are not merely background factors but active cultural frameworks that shape drinking meaning, identity, and response to alcohol harm.

The evidence also shows that Māori-specific social determinants differ from general population factors. The neighborhood study notes that area-level socioeconomic status and alcohol involvement studies produced mixed findings, and that the most consistent association was with neighborhood advantage rather than a simple SES gradient [N4-F3]. Another source on Māori-specific factors states that research suggests a co-occurring risk factor present in alcohol misuse is living in low socioeconomic areas [N2-R4]. In contrast, general population SES literature emphasizes that lower SES may be associated with greater harm rather than necessarily greater consumption, and that neighborhood advantage can increase alcohol involvement [N1-F1][N4-F3]. This means that Māori-specific determinants often operate through structural inequities, cultural identity, and community influence rather than through a single linear SES pathway. The evidence also highlights that dominant western health narratives may be culturally insensitive and that Māori conceptualisations of alcohol use need to be foregrounded [N5-F4].

In summary, colonization and historical disadvantage are foundational to current Māori drinking patterns, structural inequities in licensing and outlet distribution continue to shape exposure and harm, and whānau, tikanga, and cultural identity are essential to understanding how drinking is experienced and responded to [N2-F2][N5-F4]. Māori-specific social determinants differ from general population factors because they are mediated by cultural meaning, community structure, and historical injustice rather than only by income or education alone [N4-F3][N5-F4].
node_outputs.N9:
Policy, service access, and community-level influences on hazardous drinking

The evidence shows that access to health services and prevention programs affects drinking through both availability and community-level conditions. A neighborhood study found that living in a more advantaged and educated urban neighborhood was associated with greater alcohol involvement, and that alcohol outlet density was associated with any alcohol use but not necessarily with binge drinking or alcohol problems [N4-F3]. It also notes that access to planning and licensing processes can shape new outlet openings, and that structural barriers can limit residents’ ability to prevent them [N2-F2]. This suggests that community-level access to services, planning power, and preventive action are important influences on drinking patterns.

Neighborhood safety, housing, and social cohesion are also important. The neighborhood study found that rural versus urban residence shaped alcohol use patterns, with rural residents less likely to drink but more likely to consume more alcohol per occasion when they did [N4-F3]. It also identified neighborhood disadvantage and social disorganization theory as important contextual factors, suggesting that unsafe, unstable, or socially fragmented neighborhoods can increase drinking risk [N4-F3]. Another source states that area-level socioeconomic status is associated with levels of alcohol consumption and related harms, and that neighborhood disadvantage is linked to violence, crime, public disorder, property damage, and reduced amenity [N2-R2]. This indicates that neighborhood safety and social cohesion are not peripheral; they are part of the broader social environment that shapes drinking behavior.

What interventions are most relevant for Māori communities? The evidence points to culturally responsive and community-based interventions. The licensing study argues that licensing systems should be reviewed from equity and Indigenous perspectives and that Māori input should be recognized in decisions about alcohol [N2-F2]. The Māori treatment study reports that cultural factors and cultural identity were very highly endorsed in treatment, irrespective of age, gender, mood, or dependence level [N6-R2]. It also emphasizes the need for culturally appropriate alcohol policy and health promotion that aligns with Māori philosophical bases and secure identities [N5-F4]. A separate source on working with diversity in alcohol and other drug services notes that services should support non-government services working with the diversity of clients that access them [N5-R5]. This suggests that effective interventions for Māori communities should be community-led, culturally appropriate, and integrated with local structures and identities.

The evidence also highlights service access as a barrier. The licensing study notes that residents were largely unaware of opportunities to object to alcohol outlet licenses and faced structural barriers to accessing and influencing hearings [N2-F2]. This implies that prevention programs must be accessible and that community members need support to engage in decision-making. The Māori treatment study likewise shows that treatment effectiveness depends on cultural factors, suggesting that interventions must be designed with Māori perspectives rather than imposed from the outside [N6-R2]. The neighborhood study also shows that outlet density and neighborhood advantage can shape alcohol involvement, so prevention programs should target both availability and contextual disadvantage [N4-F3].

Overall, the most relevant interventions for Māori communities are culturally responsive, community-led, and inclusive of Māori input and tikanga. They should address neighborhood safety, housing, and social cohesion, and they should improve access to health services and prevention programs while supporting local decision-making and cultural identity [N2-F2][N4-F3][N5-F4].

Evidence on hazardous drinking patterns and methodological context

The evidence on hazardous drinking is mixed in definition and measurement. The search material does not provide a single unified definition, but it does show that hazardous drinking is often treated as a subset of alcohol-related harm or problem drinking. The neighborhood study defines alcohol involvement broadly, including any alcohol use, binge drinking, and alcohol problems, and reports that outlet density was associated with any alcohol use but not necessarily with binge drinking or alcohol problems [N4-F3]. Another source notes that hazardous drinking is part of the broader literature on alcohol-related consequences and harm [N1-F1]. This suggests that hazardous drinking is usually measured through self-reported drinking patterns, harms, or problem drinking rather than by a single standardized measure across all studies.

The evidence is not uniformly population-wide. Some studies are general population studies, while others are Māori-specific or linked to Māori communities. The SES review explicitly synthesizes data primarily from adult populations and includes population-based studies [N1-F1]. A case study on alcohol licensing in eight Aotearoa New Zealand communities is explicitly Māori-focused and examines community objections, licensing decisions, and structural barriers affecting Māori influence [N2-F2]. A separate Māori-specific study on older Māori understandings of alcohol use is also focused on indigenous perspectives and culturally specific understandings [N5-F4]. This indicates that findings are often population-wide, Māori-specific, or at least contextually focused, rather than universally generalizable.

Limitations and gaps in the evidence include weak consistency, mixed findings, and limited cultural specificity. The neighborhood study found that 68% of effects were non-significant when examining area-level socioeconomic status and alcohol use outcomes, and that there were similar proportions of significant associations with neighborhood advantage and neighborhood disadvantage [N4-F3]. The SES review notes that findings are complicated by moderating factors such as race, ethnicity, and gender, and that future studies are needed to explore underlying mechanisms [N1-F1]. Another source on Māori-specific factors states that research suggests a co-occurring risk factor is living in low socioeconomic areas, but it does not provide a detailed assessment of how hazardous drinking is defined or measured [N2-R4]. The licensing study also highlights that evidence of area deprivation supported objectors’ arguments, but a lack of official data on harms undermined them [N2-F2]. This points to gaps in measurement, data availability, and cultural specificity.

In conclusion, the evidence defines hazardous drinking through alcohol involvement, harm, or problem drinking, and measures it through self-reported or contextual indicators [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Findings are often population-wide, Māori-specific, or contextually focused rather than universally generalizable [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4]. The main limitations are mixed findings, inconsistent associations, and insufficient attention to cultural and structural contexts in some studies [N1-F1][N4-F3][N2-F2].

## Integrated explanation of the main socio-economic factors influencing hazardous drinking among Māori

The main socio-economic factors influencing hazardous drinking among Māori are best understood as a combination of income, education, neighborhood disadvantage, and broader structural and cultural context. The evidence consistently shows that socioeconomic status (SES) is one of the strongest explanatory frames, but the direction and strength of the association vary across studies, and neighborhood-level disadvantage often matters more than individual-level income alone [N1-F1][N4-F3].

### 1) Socio-economic variables most consistently associated with hazardous drinking

The most consistently associated variables are income, education, and neighborhood disadvantage/advantage. The SES literature emphasizes that people with lower SES may bear a disproportionate burden of negative alcohol-related consequences, while people with higher SES may consume similar or greater amounts of alcohol compared with lower SES groups [N1-F1]. A neighborhood study also found that living in a more advantaged and educated urban neighborhood was associated with greater alcohol involvement, although outlet density was not consistently linked to binge drinking or alcohol problems [N4-F3]. Another source notes that area-level socioeconomic status is associated with levels of alcohol consumption and related harms, and that neighborhood disadvantage is linked to violence, crime, public disorder, property damage, and reduced amenity [N2-R2].

In short, income and education are important because they are linked to greater alcohol-related harm and to contextual drinking involvement [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Neighborhood disadvantage is also important because it appears as a strong contextual determinant, while neighborhood advantage can also increase alcohol involvement [N4-F3][N4-R2].

### 2) How income, education, and employment shape drinking risk

Income is central to the evidence. The SES review explicitly notes that lower gross national income was associated with more alcohol-related consequences in men in a cross-national study, and that lower educational attainment was associated with more reported alcohol-related consequences [N1-F1]. A related source states that people with lower socioeconomic status are disproportionately affected by alcohol-related harms [N4-R3].
